title: Interval List Intersections — Two-Pointer Overlap Finding
summary: Two-pointer scanning across two independent sorted interval lists to find every overlap between them — a genuinely different pointer discipline from merging one list.

slides.markdown:
Two people each have their own sorted list of free-time blocks. Where can they actually meet? That's Interval List Intersections: given two independent, sorted, non-overlapping interval lists, find every overlap between the two.

This is not [merge-intervals](merge-intervals) again — you're not collapsing one list, you're comparing **two** lists against each other, and that calls for a genuinely different technique: a **two-pointer walk**, one pointer per list, always advancing whichever interval ends first.

It's a small mechanical shift from the earlier topics, but it's the one that most often trips up candidates who pattern-match too early and try to force a single-list merge onto a two-list problem.

Keep one pointer `i` into list A and one pointer `j` into list B. At each step, look at `A[i]` and `B[j]`:

- Compute their overlap, if any: `max(A[i].start, B[j].start)` to `min(A[i].end, B[j].end)`. If that range is valid (start `<=` end), it's an intersection — emit it.
- Then advance **whichever interval ends first** — increment `i` if `A[i].end < B[j].end`, otherwise increment `j`.

The reasoning behind "advance the earlier-ending one": once an interval's end is behind the other list's current interval, it cannot possibly overlap anything still ahead in the other list — every remaining candidate in the other list starts even later. So it's safe to retire and move on.

Picture two parallel timelines, one for list A and one for list B, each drawn as a row of non-overlapping bars. Two markers sit under the current interval in each row. At each step, the overlap between the two current bars (if any) is highlighted and emitted, then whichever bar ends first has its marker advance to the next bar in that row.

slides.sectionTitle: Losing track of which list an interval came from
slides.markdown:
A tempting shortcut: concatenate both lists into one, sort by start, and run something Merge-Intervals-like over the combined data. This throws away exactly the information the problem needs — **which original list each piece belongs to** — and merging across lists conflates "A overlaps B" with "two of A's own intervals happen to be adjacent," which shouldn't even be possible since each list is already internally non-overlapping, but the combined-and-sorted view can no longer tell the difference between within-list adjacency and cross-list overlap.

The two-pointer approach keeps the lists structurally separate the entire time — `i` only ever indexes into A, `j` only ever indexes into B — so there's never a moment where provenance is ambiguous.

slides.sectionTitle: Why discarding the earlier-ending interval is safe
slides.markdown:
The correctness of "advance whichever interval ends first" rests on one fact: both lists are sorted by start and internally non-overlapping. If `A[i]` ends before `B[j]` does, then every interval still ahead in A — `A[i+1]`, `A[i+2]`, …, — starts even later than `A[i]` did (sortedness), so it starts even later relative to `B[j]`'s current position too.

That means `A[i]` has no unfinished business: it has already been compared against `B[j]`, and it cannot possibly overlap anything B has coming up that starts later than `B[j]` does. It's safe to retire permanently. This is the same "no need to look back" guarantee that made the single-list merge pass work — here it just applies across two lists instead of one.

| | Merge Intervals | Interval List Intersection |
|---|---|---|
| Inputs | One list | Two independent lists |
| Pointer discipline | One index, extend-or-close | Two indices, advance whichever ends first |
| What's tracked | A single "current merge" range | The overlap between two current ranges |
| Sort needed? | Yes, O(n log n) | No — both lists already sorted, O(n + m) |

They look similar because both are "sorted-interval sweeps," but the actual invariant being maintained is different: one tracks a *running union*, the other tracks *pairwise overlap between two independent sequences*. Reaching for the wrong one on the wrong problem is the most common mix-up in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: A single point can be a valid intersection
slides.markdown:
`[1,3]` and `[3,5]` produce `lo = max(1,3) = 3` and `hi = min(3,5) = 3` — a zero-width intersection at the single point 3. Whether that counts as a real intersection depends on the same touching-boundary convention seen in [merge-intervals](merge-intervals): if the problem treats intervals as closed ranges `[start, end]`, a single shared point is a legitimate intersection and the `lo <= hi` check correctly includes it.

If the problem instead uses half-open ranges, you'd want `lo < hi` to exclude single-point touches. Missing this distinction either fabricates intersections that shouldn't exist or silently drops legitimate ones — always confirm which convention the interviewer means before locking in the comparison operator.

slides.sectionTitle: Complexity and why no sort is needed
slides.markdown:
**O(n + m)** time, where n and m are the lengths of the two lists, and **O(1)** auxiliary space beyond the output — no sort call anywhere, because the problem hands you sorted lists as a precondition.

This is worth stating explicitly in an interview: candidates who reflexively reach for `sorted()` on inputs that are already documented as sorted are spending an unnecessary O(n log n) or O(m log m) for nothing, the same mistake covered in [insert-interval](insert-interval). Recognizing "the precondition already gives me what I need" and skipping redundant work is a recurring signal across this entire group.

This two-pointer, advance-the-earlier-ender pattern generalizes past intervals: it's the same shape used to merge two sorted linked lists, to intersect two sorted arrays, or to join two sorted streams in a database's merge-join operator. Whenever you have two independently sorted sequences and need to find where they relate — overlap, match, or merge — reach for two pointers advancing in lockstep before reaching for anything that requires combining and re-sorting.

A staff-level answer to "how would this scale to many lists, not just two" points toward a k-way merge with a heap holding the current front of each list — the same idea Skyline and k-way merge problems build on later.
